## Exact assumptions and conditional bounds

- [`sat26-general`](../../ASSUMPTIONS.md#sat26-general)
- [`sat26-reported-formal`](../../ASSUMPTIONS.md#sat26-reported-formal)
- [`sat26-sparse`](../../ASSUMPTIONS.md#sat26-sparse)

Conditional on `sat26-general`:

$$
2^{O(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}L^{O(1)}
$$

Alternatively, conditional on `sat26-reported-formal`:

$$
2^{O(n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n})}L^{O(1)}
$$

The resulting algorithm is deterministic and uses polynomial space, conditional on the corresponding assumption and this derivation. $L$ denotes the original input length; constants may depend on the stated fixed constants. Logarithms in asymptotic bounds may be regularized when the declared measure is small.

## Preprocessing

Retain declared variables even if unused. Treat impossible nullary constraints immediately.

## Encoding size

| Quantity | Bound |
| --- | --- |
| Boolean variables, including auxiliaries | $qn$ |
| Clauses | $O_{q,r}(n+m)$ |
| Maximum clause width | $\max\{q,r,2\}$ |

## Derivation

1. Use one-hot bits for the q possible values of each original variable, with exactly-one constraints.

2. For every forbidden tuple of a constraint, add a clause forbidding its one-hot value combination. Each relation has at most q^r tuples, a constant; each tuple clause has width at most r.

3. Every CSP assignment corresponds to exactly one Boolean assignment. There are qn variables and O_{q,r}(n+m) fixed-width clauses, so apply the general-density counting profile.

4. When m=O(n), the sparse profile gives B(n) times a polynomial factor. Fixed-target graph homomorphism and list homomorphism are included as binary-CSP examples.

## Caveats and comparison limits

- The constants q and r must be fixed. Succinct relations or growing domains require a separate analysis.
- This is a direct encoding of the entire instance, not elimination of a modulator that loses extension multiplicities.

Counting requires a count-preserving encoding and preprocessing, or an explicit correction for multiplicities. The derivation must justify this; decision preservation alone is insufficient.
